title: AI-Assisted Businesses
summary: You set the goal → AI drafts → You check, then publish
subtitle: Use AI as your fast assistant, and keep yourself as the boss.

blocks.text: AI tools can draft, sum up, design and answer questions in seconds. They can also state something wrong with total confidence, like a coworker who never says “I’m not sure.” This lesson shows you how to use that speed without lending your name to its mistakes.
Get hours back each week without handing over your judgement.
blocks.detail: You will learn a simple draft, decide, and check routine that makes you faster while keeping your customers’ trust.
blocks.extra: Section 05 walks you through that routine one step at a time.

blocks.text: Generative AI is software that makes new text, images or sound by following patterns learned from huge amounts of existing work. It does not know your business the way you do, and it has no idea whether its answer is true. It just writes what sounds likely.

In an AI-assisted business, you do the thinking and the tool speeds up the routine work: first drafts, product notes, replies to customers, images and spreadsheet formulas. You stay responsible for everything that goes out under your name.
One rule keeps this safe and easy to remember: the AI drafts, you decide, and you check. Skip any of those three steps and trouble starts.

sections.title: What to hand over, what to keep

items.title: Product descriptions
list: What AI can do: Write a first draft
What you must do: Fix the facts, the tone, and any claims

items.title: Customer replies
list: What AI can do: Suggest wording
What you must do: Read it before sending, and never let it promise anything you cannot deliver

items.title: Logos and images
list: What AI can do: Offer many options quickly
What you must do: Check that nothing looks like a real brand’s artwork

items.title: Tax, money, or legal questions
list: What AI can do: Help you prepare good questions
What you must do: Confirm every answer with the CRA or a qualified professional

items.title: Customer personal information
list: What you must do: Keep it out of tools that your business does not control

blocks.text: Check every number, date and source. AI tools can make up facts, links and even laws that sound real. Treat every figure and citation as unchecked until you have checked it yourself, most of all anything about tax or the law.
Who owns AI-made work?

In Canada, it is unclear who owns work made fully by AI. A 2021 copyright filing listed a person and an AI painting app as co-authors, but the office does not review filings, and the courts have not settled the question. The United States requires a human author. In practice, add real human work to anything you plan to build your brand on.

Read the tool’s terms before you rely on it. Look for two answers: who may use what the tool makes for you, and whether the words you type in are used to train the tool. Many tools let you turn training off in the settings. Pick a paid or business plan when you work with client material.

items.title: “If the AI wrote it, nobody can blame me for the mistakes.”
items.text: The business that posts the content is responsible for it. The Competition Act bans false or misleading claims in marketing, whether a person or a program wrote the words.

blocks.text: Privacy and honest claims

Customer names, emails and money details are personal information, and federal privacy law (PIPEDA) still applies when you paste them into a tool. Canada’s privacy regulators have shared joint principles for generative AI. A good habit is to keep customer data out of any tool you do not control.

Be careful with labels like “AI-powered” or “guaranteed results.” Overstating what AI does in your business is called AI washing. It can break the same rules against misleading ads that apply to any other claim.

Good practice: be open about chatbots. No rule in this lesson says every business must label its AI help, but honesty is cheap. If a chatbot answers your customers, say that it is a chatbot, and make it easy to reach a real person.

Watch out for “earn with AI” offers. The Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre warns about job offers that ask you to boost or finish online tasks, then push you to deposit money you can never take out. Quebec’s consumer office adds a simple test: be wary of anyone who asks for money before you can work.
Read It Twice
paragraphs: Karim Nasser ran a small cleaning company in Calgary, and he wanted to buy a second van. To do that, he needed ten more clients. His mother had given him a fridge magnet years ago that read, “Read it twice.” He had never paid it any attention.
Karim started using an AI tool to write quotes and answer customer messages. It was fast, and he loved it. Replies that once took an hour now took five minutes, and the clients seemed happy.

One busy Friday, a customer asked about a deep clean. The tool wrote a warm reply that promised same-day service and a full refund for any reason. Karim was tired, and the message sounded great. He pressed send without reading it.

On Monday the customer wrote back. She wanted her same-day service and she meant to hold him to it. Karim stared at the screen. He could say, “The AI wrote that, not me.” Or he could take responsibility.

He called her, apologized, and kept the promise that one time. It cost him a full day and several hundred dollars. Then he sat down and made a plan. Every AI draft would be checked for prices, dates, and promises before it went out. He wrote a short list of things the tool must never promise, and he pasted it into each prompt.

The twist surprised him. The customer posted a review that said, “He made a mistake and he fixed it. That is rare.” She sent three of her neighbours his way. By spring Karim had his ten new clients and his second van. On his monitor sat a sticky note with three words in his mother’s style: Read it twice.

blocks.text: Owning a mistake is a business skill, and a short checklist makes it easy.
blocks.detail: A clear routine keeps your speed, protects your reputation, and turns an AI slip into a story that customers trust.
blocks.extra: Section 05 gives you the checklist that Karim wished he had.

items.title: State the job clearly.
items.text: Tell the tool exactly what you want, who the reader is, and what it must never promise.

items.title: Let the AI draft.
items.text: Treat the result as a rough first version and nothing more.

items.title: Check the facts and the promises.
items.text: Verify every price, date, number, name, and guarantee against your own records.

items.title: Remove private information.
items.text: Do not paste customers’ personal details into tools that your business does not control.

items.title: Keep a simple record.
items.text: Save what you published, which tool helped, and who approved it.

items.title: Report your earnings.
items.text: Money from AI-assisted work is still business income. Report it on Form T2125 with your tax return.

blocks.text: Notes by province, and for your taxes

items.title: Privacy
items.text: PIPEDA covers most businesses, but Alberta, British Columbia and Quebec have their own private-sector privacy laws. Check the one that applies to you.

items.title: Quebec customers
items.text: Quebec’s Consumer Protection Act also bans false or misleading claims, and French-language rules apply to marketing aimed at Quebecers.

items.title: GST/HST
items.text: You must register once your taxable sales pass $30,000 in one calendar quarter, or over the last four quarters added together. Below that, registering is optional.

items.title: “Earning money with AI is just a hobby, so it is not taxed.”
items.text: The CRA says to report all income from all sources, and the tool that helped you earn it does not change that.

blocks.text: Insider tip: Keep a “never promise” list beside your AI tool. Cover refunds, deadlines, prices, results, and tax or legal advice. Paste it into every prompt, then read the draft before it goes out.
Quick Check

items.title: Who is responsible for an AI-written reply that you send to a customer?
items.detail: You are, because you published it.

items.title: Is it safe to paste a customer’s full details into any free AI tool?
items.text: Keep personal information out of tools that you do not control.

items.title: Is it clear in Canada who owns artwork made entirely by AI?
items.text: The question is still unsettled.

blocks.text: Knowledge Check

items.title: What does the “check” step involve? A. Trusting the tool because it sounds confident · B. Verifying facts, numbers, and promises before anything is published · C. Asking the AI whether it was right
items.text: Only you can confirm what is true for your business.

items.title: Which information should stay out of a public AI tool? A. Your product descriptions · B. Customers’ names, emails, and financial details · C. A general question about marketing
items.text: Personal information stays protected under privacy law, even when a tool is convenient.

items.title: An offer says you can earn money by completing AI tasks, but first you must deposit funds. What should you do? A. Deposit a small amount to test it · B. Treat it as a likely scam and do not pay · C. Share it with friends
items.text: Being asked to pay before you can earn is a common fraud pattern.

items.title: Write one rule you will follow every time you use AI for work.
items.text: I will read every draft twice and check each price, date, and promise before I send it.

blocks.text: The AI drafts, you decide, and you check. Keep customer data private, and never promise what you have not verified.

items.title: Generative AI
items.text: Software that creates new text, images, or audio from patterns in existing material.

items.title: Prompt
items.text: The instructions that you give an AI tool.

items.title: Hallucination
items.text: A confident answer from an AI tool that is wrong or made up.

items.title: AI washing
items.text: Overstating the role or power of AI in a product or service.

items.title: Personal information
items.text: Any information about an identifiable person, such as a name or an email address.

items.title: Human review
items.text: A person checking AI work before it is used or posted.
